#8258. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8253. UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

The 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

For the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:

Race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

Two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI announced the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”

The discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its new mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

The 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

This will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

From the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti says. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”

But coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti says. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he says.

Overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB.  “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”

American Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”

If there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne said.

For spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”

Could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this new schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour company Run the Alps.

#8251. A Thanksgiving Blizzard Pushed Big Mule Deer Off the Mountain — and Down to Us

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 25, 2026 9:23 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 issue of Outdoor Life.

For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S. Forest Service trail to avoid hunting through the dense evergreen woods on both sides. There the trees sagged under heavy burdens of snow, and to brush against just one branch was to release a load of it down the back of my neck.

But following the trail wasn’t always easy. In places the blaze marks were obliterated by snow that a high wind had plastered against the tree trunks, and here and there drifts were piled waist-high. Slogging through such deep wet snow can take the joy out of deer hunting, so I decided to head back for the warmth and comfort of the ranch. I elected to take a shortcut rather than to retrace my steps, and that decision proved to be a mistake.

My shortcut led down and around a slope, then crossed an old burned area, now grown up in a thicket, where the new snow covered a nightmare of crisscrossed deadfalls. Before I reached the far side of the burn, I tripped many times and was wet from chest to toes. I swore out loud the last time I fell, and in that instant three does suddenly sprung from their beds in the snow and fled downhill.

The does did not bounce away in the characteristic stiff-legged manner of mule deer. Instead they hesitated and floundered, now and then up to their bellies in the snow. I threw the rifle to my shoulder and could easily have shot all three, so slow was their progress. But the purpose of my trip was to bag one good buck, and I had a few more days to hunt.

Back in camp, I found George Smith and John Moxley propping wet boots close to a cast-iron stove to dry while a pot of coffee brewed on top.

“We may have started this hunt too late,” John added.

I almost had to agree with John — the three does were the only deer I had seen since arriving at George Smith’s Canyon Creek Ranch. For years George has been guiding hunters from this ranch, located in the Pioneer Mountains of the Beaverhead National Forest, about 17 miles of steep winding road from Melrose, Montana. When John and I couldn’t make our annual Western hunt in time for the October opening of the big-game season, George suggested that we hold off until the season’s last week, which would be the last week in November.

“By that time,” he had written, “the big bucks should be down low and we can have a real trophy hunt. Besides, all my guests will have gone home for Thanksgiving, so Bob and I can join you.”

Bob is my youngest son, and he was working for the Smith family during the season as a guide and wrangler.

The plan sounded perfect to John and me. John is from Ohio, and I had recently moved from Ohio to Wyoming.

On a crisp bright day in November — perfect weather for big-game hunting — I met John at the airport in Butte, Montana. We picked up some supplies and then drove the 60 miles to Canyon Creek Ranch. We arrived well after dusk under a still-clear sky.

I’d never felt more optimistic about starting a hunt. But two things did bother me. First, we did not see any deer in the headlights of our vehicle on the drive to the ranch. Second, after our arrival George mentioned seeing a great gray owl around the ranch buildings. In that region the great gray is a rare visitor, and according to George it arrives only ahead of a storm.

“The last gray owl I saw,” George recalled, “came just before the worst winter storm in my memory hit this place.”

Late that night, snow began to fall and a violent wind came up. The snow didn’t stop until more than a foot of white covered the high country — about 7,000 feet at the Canyon Creek Ranch — and the temperature plunged to zero. We did very little hunting, and it was unsuccessful.

“The deer have either bedded down until the blast passes,” George explained, “or moved down to where the snow isn’t so deep. We’ll have to wait and see.”

At first the waiting wasn’t too bad. I hadn’t seen Bob or George for a year, and we had plenty of stories to swap in the snug ranch atmosphere. Besides, there was a Thanksgiving banquet to cook and eat. But eventually I got restless and wanted to start hunting in spite of the conditions. The result was that we left a good many bootprints in the deep snow without covering much distance or seeing any deer or even any game sign.

The morning after I saw the does, I started out early. The wind had stopped blowing, but visibility was still poor. Gray clouds hung in the canyons and close to the wooded slopes so that long-range scanning with binoculars was seldom possible. One very effective tactic for hunting in good snow cover in mountainous country is to carefully glass all slopes, particularly south slopes, for game that stands out sharply against the white. The clouds ruled out that tactic.

But the day didn’t pass without excitement. I had crossed a steep draw and, on reaching level ground on the far side, had paused to catch my breath. A moment later I heard animals crashing toward me through an evergreen thicket up ahead. My heart began to pound. I flipped off the safety on my Model 700 Remington 7 mm. Magnum and held the rifle ready. A cow moose followed by a calf stomped into the open and crossed my path without even a sidelong glance in my direction. It was quite a surprise to see them so far from more-typical moose habitat.

Bob had good news back at the ranch that night. He had scouted in another direction and found many tracks.

“They seem to be paralleling Canyon Creek, heading down toward the old ghost camp,” Bob said. “If the snow’s thinner, we might find them there tomorrow.”

The next morning was bitterly cold. We gathered in the ranch kitchen and huddled around the cook stove while George carved thick strips of bacon from a slab and mixed up a large bowl of sourdough pancake batter. It is a standard practical joke around Canyon Creek to conceal a round sheet of cardboard inside some unsuspecting diner’s pancake and then watch him try to cut it with a fork. George pulled the trick on John, and we had a good laugh before beginning a cold day.

It was possible to drive our four-wheel-drive rig partway to where Bob had found sign the day before. We parked our vehicle beside a small tributary of Canyon Creek, now almost completely frozen, and followed it on foot to an open meadow bordered by a wooded slope. There we found Bob’s tracks as well as deer tracks that had been made since his reconnaissance. It was soon evident that a herd of deer had fed along the meadow’s edges; in windswept places they had pawed circular areas free of snow to get at the vegetation underneath. But apparently the deer hadn’t lingered long, and their tracks disappeared in many different directions.

“Our best bet,” George said, “is to go separate ways and see what we find.”

Because George knew the country best, he took a more complicated route, which led through heavy cover, wound around a mountainside, and nearly dead-ended at a steep rocky cliff. He figured that game might be bedded on top or near the face of the cliff.

John and I proceeded together until the meandering tracks appeared to divide into two small herds. Then we separated, planning to meet late in the day on an unimproved road far below.

One set of the tracks I followed was very large, and I concentrated on it. I walked parallel to the buck’s path on the downwind side while watching far ahead for a glimpse of the animal. That technique had worked well for me on other hunts, and it might work again.

I was so intent on following the buck that I almost stumbled over a bedded doe. She went flying in a cloud of snow down the slope. Then, before my hands were steady again, a shot cracked in the distance. The shot spooked a second deer about 150 yards to my right. I saw the animal for only an instant and couldn’t tell whether it was my buck. But when I hurried back to the buck’s trail, I found the spot where he had suddenly shifted into high gear.

For the rest of the day I stillhunted slowly but got no action. I was optimistic, however, for at last we were in deer country.

The shot I’d heard was George’s. He had broken the ice. About a mile from where he’d left John and me, he’d noticed that the tracks of the largest deer became more meandering — often an indication that a deer is seeking a good place to bed. George slowed his own pace accordingly, stopping often to scan thoroughly every bit of mountain terrain in front of him. This is the simplest and oldest of all mule-deer-hunting strategies, and once again it paid off.

Just before George reached a small draw, he stopped. Soon he saw a shape that put him on alert. On the slope slightly above him was the outline of a buck’s rack, somewhat obscured by a screen of brush. In the next moment the deer was on its feet and running. But it was slowed by snow, and it hadn’t gone more than 20 feet when George drilled a shot through the lungs. He found the animal dead 50 yards from where it had been hit.

The buck was an old, heavy five-pointer (Western count) with unusually heavy beams. It was a trophy that even an old-timer in the Montana Rockies could brag about. The buck, even when field-dressed, was a terrible weight to drag to the nearest pickup point. Without the slippery snow and all-downhill going, we would have needed a packhorse or two for the job.

But the day produced more than a trophy mule deer for George. It also revealed that deer were moving from the high country into lower ranges where food was more available. The farther we had hunted that day, the more fresh tracks we had encountered. John reported jumping 12 deer from a sheltered meadow that, from the amount of tracks and digging in the snow, resembled a livestock pasture. None of the deer had the kind of rack that John was looking for, but his gloom early in the trip had been replaced by enthusiasm.

“Tomorrow,” he predicted to me, “both of us will score.”

The next morning was overcast, and flurries of snow drifted to the ground as we huddled again around the kitchen stove. After breakfast George drove us to a spot close to where John had seen deer the day before. We had driven along that same trail several times before. Only two days before, John noted, the only track on the new snow had been made by a wandering coyote. Now deer tracks were everywhere.

George left John and me where the road forked. He would pick us up late in the afternoon at a point about two miles farther on.

Few thrills can match walking through woodlands that you know contain game. You are tense and excited, and it’s difficult to slow down and hunt carefully enough.

John and I had scarcely separated when I saw deer running over an open ridge ahead and above me. I didn’t spot any antlers, but no matter. All the animals were out of range and gone before I would have had a shot.

“Slow down,” I said to myself half-aloud. But my pulse was racing.

That day I saw as many muleys as I’ve ever seen on a day’s hunt afoot. We had found a winter deer yard, and collecting venison would have been incredibly easy. But I kept hoping for the big buck. Actually I did see two together, but they were traveling and already 400 to 500 yards away.

At dusk when I came out again on the road, weary to the bone, I still hadn’t fired a shot. The headlights of George’s vehicle were a welcome sight in the gloom. Even better was the big buck lashed on top. John had scored, and back at the ranch he told about it.

Early in the morning, after his eagerness had spooked a very good buck, John decided to hunt more from the seat of his pants and less by hiking all over the landscape. When he found a good sheltered place, he sat down on a deadfall. Though the mountain slope opposite him seemed empty of game, he studied it through his glasses. Soon he focused on a spike buck, bedded and almost hidden behind a juniper bush. John shifted his gaze slightly upward, and there he saw the kind of buck he wanted.

The four-pointer was bedded in a cluster of trees and was in deep shadow. But his antlers, outlined against the snow, gave him away. John figured that the range was more than 500 yards — much too far to risk a shot — but that by making good use of the cover on his side of the mountain he could cut the distance in half. He made the stalk successfully, and one shot from his Model 700 Remington .30/06 anchored the buck.

That left one day — the last day of the open season — for me to score.

Perhaps because of the intense cold in the bunkhouse the next morning, the alarm clock didn’t work and George had to awaken me.

“Look out the window,” he called, “and over toward Canyon Creek.”

There, in the crown of a dead spruce splintered long ago by lightning, sat the great gray owl. Probably another storm was on its way. As a result I wolfed my breakfast and, though I should have known better, got hooked on one of George’s cardboard pancakes.

George drove me close to the deer yard we had found, and from there I started out on foot. It was not a pleasant morning to be afield. Scattered snow flurries were being driven by a wild bitter wind, which was quickly obliterating deer tracks and which made cautious hunting — stopping often to scan the slopes — very difficult. I had to keep moving to keep warm. By mid-morning I had found very few fresh tracks and had seen no deer. I figured that all or at least most of the deer had already moved to even lower elevations ahead of the new storm. My chances looked very poor.

At noon I found some deadfalls on the edge of a dense spruce thicket that furnished a fairly good windbreak, and I sat down to munch a sandwich and a candy bar. The place also gave me a good view, between snow squalls, of distant, partly timbered mountainsides. Through binoculars I examined the wooded slopes, concentrating on those farthest away. As I glassed, I caught a slight movement much closer. Refocusing the glasses, I saw a forkhorn traveling slowly down the hill below me. He was less than 200 yards away, and though the crosswind wasn’t the best for shooting, it would not give me away.

I decided I would have to take the forkhorn or get nothing at all. Slowly I raised my rifle and found a rest for it on the deadfall. The shot would have been easy, but as I was about to squeeze off, a second forkhorn strolled out into the open. Then, right behind him, came a third buck.

At first I could see only the body of the third buck in my scope. But that was enough to tell me he was big. As I watched, the buck changed direction and was hidden from view again. Should I take a chance and play the waiting game, or shoot one of the forkhorns, still in sight?

The big buck resolved my indecision when he appeared again. This time I could see his splendid rack. My 7 mm. was sighted-in for 200 yards, so I held the crosshairs on the point of the shoulder, adjusted for windage, and squeezed. The deer lurched forward, out of view; I didn’t know whether I’d connected.

I hurried down the steep slope and waded through a deep drift in a gully. I found the buck lying dead against a tree trunk. He was a fine four-pointer and as heavy a mule deer as I’ve ever bagged.

That evening the great gray owl proved to be an accurate prophet. Another storm pounded the Rockies and plastered the high country with another layer of snow. But back at the ranch, I barely noticed it.

“The idea of the late hunt,” John said, “was sure a great one.”

A Montana nonresident big-game license costs $151. A deer-only license, which entitles the holder to one deer in a specified district, is $35, plus $1 for a conservation license. This year the general season on deer in Montana runs from October 22 to November 26. But prospective hunters should write the Montana Fish and Game Department, Helena, Montana 59601, for a copy of the detailed hunting regulations.

Read Next: I Promised to Take My Boys Rabbit Hunting Every Day of Christmas Break

The tag end of the season can be a good time for any big-game hunt. Almost everywhere in the West, the odds for connecting with a trophy head may be improved then, simply because the animals are not so high and are easier to find. Of course, there are unseasonably warm years when animals are not driven downward by deep snow until after the season ends. Remember too that late-season hunting can be very rugged — and occasionally impossible. It’s wise to know bad-weather and snow-survival techniques. But these are the chances a sportsman must take. And for my money, the rewards are worth the gamble.

The Huk Rogue Wave deck boots are arguably the most popular fishing boots out there, and for good reason. They’re completely waterproof, lightweight, durable, and, most importantly, comfortable enough to wear all day on your feet. The grippy outsoles provide plenty of traction on even the most slippery surfaces (like wet boat decks and piers), too.

When the weather warms up and they drop the boat in, they’re going to need a good pair of fishing shorts. And for that, we give you these from AFTCO. Not only are they stain-resistant and well-made, they feature a stretchy waistband for comfort and a lined pocket for sharp tools like pliers. Available in 15 colors from navy and khaki to coral and turquoise, they come in sizes 28 to 46.

I’m a firm believer you can’t have too many coffee mugs. This speckled stoneware cup features the iconic Bass Pro logo along with a generous 16-ounce capacity for your morning brew.

Forward-facing sonar is one of the coolest and also most controversial trends of the year. Thus, the Berkley Finisher FFS bait is sure to be a crowd-pleasing gift (and a conversation starter!). It’s highly versatile for a range of applications and will lead your giftee right to where all the fish are biting.

If your fly fishing friend wants to start tying their own flies, they’ll love this White River Fly Shop kit. It has everything they need to get started in the art of fly tying, including pliers, scissors, bobbins, tweezers, and other essential tools. An added bonus? It all comes neatly packed in a sleek wood carrying case.

These retractable fishing line snips are a total game-changer. No more using bulky scissors or rusted nail clippers. The corrosion-resistant stainless steel blade may be small but it’s mighty—it can easily cut through up to 50-pound test line. Plus, it hooks right onto their pocket or vest for easy access.

One of our experts’ favorite fish scales, this digital one from Bass Pro is a must-have for measuring their next catch, with a 50-pound weight capacity and easy-to-read scale. After all, if you don’t get to brag about how big that smallmouth was, does it even count?

There are regular fillet knives, and then there are electric fillet knives. The latter gets the job done with less time and less effort—just what any angler wants. This cordless knife from Bubba boasts a comfortable non-slip grip and a durable blade that’s equal parts sturdy and flexible.

Any angler would be thrilled to unwrap a pair of Costa sunglasses. One of the most popular styles from the eyewear brand is the Fantail. The polarized glass lenses are scratch-resistant and designed to increase contrast while blocking glare, so your giftee can easily zero in on their next catch. They come in four frame colors and two lens colors.

Give them everything they need to clean their catch with this all-in-one fillet kit. They’ll get two stainless steel fillet knives (7- and 9-inch), a cut-resistant glove for safe handling, a knife sharpener to keep those blades razor sharp, a stainless steel odor bar for washing their hands afterwards, and a roll-up sleeve for storage.

Maybe you’re getting a gift for a bass nut. Not as stuffy as the fly fisherman, but just as (maybe more) obsessive about their gear. Abu Garcia’s Revo5 X is our standout baitcaster. You can rip lures in with a 10.1:1 gear ratio—pulling in 41-feet of line with a single turn. Internally, you’ve got 10+1 corrosion-resistant bearings to keep things smooth. Externally, you’ve got a super tough alloy frame and side plates. It’s lightweight, durable, and capable. Everything your bass bum needs.

Give them an easy way to keep all their lures, lines, and tools organized on the go with this tackle bag backpack. It’s made of UV- and water-resistant material so it’ll hold up for years to come and it has enough interior storage space to hold up to 11 tackle boxes. Bonus: It comes with four boxes to get them started.

A landing net can be a great asset to any fisherman or woman. This one conveniently folds up to make it more compact and easy to stash on your boat or kayak. The rubberized net prevents tangles and doesn’t damage even the rowdiest of fish thrashing around.

Sunburn is an easy way to ruin a good day of fishing. Protect them from the sun’s rays with this popular booney hat from Columbia. The combination of the wide brim and quick-drying, UPF 50 material offers ample coverage, while the breathable mesh will keep them nice and cool.

For those days when they want to relax as much as they want to fish, gift them this lounger fishing chair. It’s lightweight yet heavy duty with padded armrests and a headrest for added comfort. The adjustable rod holders, water-resistant fabric, and under-seat pocket just for tackle boxes makes it a no-brainer for lazy afternoons on the bank.

Multi tools always make a good gift for anyone interested in the outdoors or who just likes to do maintenance projects at home. The Gerber Dual-Force comes with eleven different tools and a well-made 3.25-inch steel blade.  —SM

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

Highlights Education Amanda graduated from Wake Forest University in North Carolina with a Bachelor of Science in business management and finance. Experience Amanda taught herself how to shoot a bow when she was bored one day—and a new obsession was born. Since then, she’s fallen in love with bowhunting and later waterfowl hunting (thanks to her husband who took her on her first duck hunt in 2020!). Amanda came to Field & Stream in August 2022 from USA Today with nearly a decade of commerce and product testing experience. She’s passionate about the outdoors and spends as much time as she can shooting her bow, hunting with her husband at Hart-Miller Island, and hiking with their German shepherd. Favorite Gear I love my Mr. Heater Portable Buddy Heater. It’s lightweight and portable, heats up in seconds, and has saved me on many a frigid duck hunting mornings when we’re in the jon boat or blind. Notable Work

#8249. Hunting Unpressured Bucks on One of the Best Properties in the Country

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 25, 2026 11:51 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

We are well into deer season now, and bucks are definitely feeling the pressure. If you’re like the rest of us, you’re probably seeing daylight movement start to decrease on your trail cameras, or maybe it’s already dropped off. I’m right there with you. The places that I hunt see plenty of pressure, even though they’re on private ground. This week on the podcast, I’m talking to our gear editor, Scott Einsmann, who just came back from an incredibly unique experience: He was hunting almost completely unpressured mature bucks in the Midwest. Scott shares what that experience was like, what he learned from it, and how it can help him — and you — back in the real world of deer hunting. —Alex Robinson, editor-in-chief

Listen to this episode on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Alex Robinson: Hey, Scott, thanks for joining the Outdoor Life Podcast. I want to talk to you about your favorite thing in the world, which is bowhunting for whitetail deer.

Scott Einsmann: Awesome. Let’s do it. I just came off the most amazing week of bowhunting for whitetails.

Alex: Yeah. We’re coming up on the holiday season, and you have a good redemption story, and everybody loves a good redemption story around the holidays. So to start this off, explain the property that you’re able to hunt in Illinois. What’s it like, and how did you weasel your way into getting bowhunting access to this place?

Scott: It’s 800 acres in southern Illinois, and what makes it a really good 800 acres is, one, it has topography, and it also has large wood blocks in it, and it’s surrounded by big ag fields. So once all the crops are cut, all the deer get sucked right into this property. For that reason, it’s just insane hunting. There are really good deer. There’s not a 200-incher on it, but there are a ton of 130- to 150-inch deer, and a ton of really good 8-points — some really cool deer. Last year, some big 6-points were killed, which is always fun. And maybe 300 does just running around this place. I mean, it’s crazy.

Alex: So talk about whose property it is and how you’re able to get on it, because you’re not a multimillionaire property owner.

Alex: A lot of these properties are either owned or leased by — you know, it’s the stuff that everybody dreams about hunting, but not everybody really gets access to.

Scott: Yes. And I did inquire with the farm manager there: How does someone get a lease in this area? You really just have to know the local farmers, because a lot of them have been burned by people leasing their property and not treating it right. So you really have to have someone to vouch for you and then be part of the community.

Luckily, I know someone. Levi Morgan and Andy Morgan have the lease for this property, and they have several leases in the area now, and they’re all pretty incredible. But this one they’ve had the longest — about three years now — and they’re really starting to dial it in and understand how the deer use it. They’re connected with our friends at Tactacam Reveal, and part of being an outdoor writer is you get to go on press trips.

Press trips vary in quality and fun. But this one is by far the best I’ve ever been on, because it’s not a guided hunt. You’re not just being driven around by an outfitter and sitting over a corn pile somewhere. We go out there in the summer, we hang stands, we hang cameras, get to learn the property a little bit, and then we have access to those cameras all season long — which for me is great, because my home lease is not that exciting by comparison.

Scott: So just being able to scroll and see cool deer after cool deer — and they have a ton of turkeys as well, and I have some good news there. So we have access to all that, and then we come back in November and hunt the place during the peak of the rut.

And it is so much fun to be in a place where you get to see whitetail deer acting like whitetail deer, because it gets hunted two weeks out of the year, by bowhunters only. There’s no gun hunting on it. So it’s a big property with very limited pressure, and these deer act like deer. They’re out in the middle of the day. There’s this one field right by the hog barn, and there’s a little strip of beans in it, but the rest is wheat or rye or something like that. It’s a huge field. At 1 o’clock in the afternoon on any given day, there’s a dozen does out there, and there’s probably going to be a buck checking every one of those does. It’s a really hard place to kill a deer, but it’s a fun place to watch deer.

It’s just an example. There are just deer out like that. In my area, in the Southeast, you would never see that, because someone’s going to take a shot at those deer from the road.

Alex: Yeah, I mean, even my area of Wisconsin and Minnesota — you’ve got a couple people hunting every, say, 80 acres, right? If you split up all the farmland around my area of western Wisconsin, there’s probably one hunter per 80 acres hunting pretty much every weekend. Some of those guys are very good hunters and they’re holding out for big bucks. Other folks are just out there for fun and they’re going to shoot whatever. There’s a lot in between, but there is hunting pressure basically from October through the heart of the gun season, which we’re in right now.

We have private property in north-central Wisconsin that my family always hunts, and opening day of gun season, it’s like a war zone. You just hear gunfire from all directions echoing through the morning, basically that entire first day. You can see the neighbors on their properties. Some folks will sit right on the property line. And even though we’re hunting private land, the deer know that they’re being hunted, and it’s a high-pressure situation. And that’s not even considering public land, right? So you have this view into a world that very few —

Alex: Very few places even exist like this, where deer can just be deer throughout basically the fall cycle.

Scott: Yeah, pretty much. And I’m lucky to be at a place in my hunting career where I really, really appreciate it. I know how good it is and how lucky I am.

Alex: So this is your second crack at it this season. And not to dredge up the dark times, but I feel like enough time has passed now: You hunted out there last season. Talk about what went down.

Scott: So last season, one, we didn’t hit the chase period — the rut — as well as we did this year. So we weren’t really seeing a ton of deer, by the standards of this place in Illinois.

Scott: This was maybe day three or so. I had sat a stand on this cool little food plot that we have down there, and some guy just ends up walking in on the setup around 8 or 9 o’clock in the morning.

Scott: Yes, trespassing into it. I took a picture of him real quick and shot a text to Levi and Andy, who had already killed their deer, so they were just helping everybody else kill. They said they would be there lickety-split. We said hi to the guy, and he looked up like a doe who just realized that you were there. Just busted. And he said, “Oh, sorry,” and then he left. I was like, “That was so weird. I don’t know who that was or what they were doing here.”

And it turns out that in Andy and Levi’s truck was the farm manager, John, who is a character all of his own. We should do a documentary about him. He’s such an interesting individual. So they’re pulling in, and they see this guy leaving where we’re at. Before the truck even stops, John is out of the truck running up to this guy, and he just unloads a verbal assault on him. Andy and Levi are in the truck in shock, like, “Oh my God, is there about to be a huge fight?” But this guy understood that he was in the wrong, and he backed off, apologized and left. Turns out he was living next door, and they believe he was being evicted, and they think he was coming to look for something to steal before he left.

Alex: So, like, maybe trying to grab some trail cameras or —

Scott: Yeah, trail cameras or something, whatever. Not the most upstanding citizen of McLeansboro, Illinois.

Alex: OK. All right. So we’ve got this going on in the middle of your hunt.

Scott: Yeah. So that spot is blown, but I’m watching trail camera feeds nonstop. And that morning, there was a good deer in this food plot just up the hill from where we were sitting, and we had seen him from that spot. They were like, “He might come back there this evening. Let’s try to get into that stand.” So we get up there. It’s called Liquid Death, and it’s right next to a plot called Andy’s Plot. So you have these two food plots that are right next to each other, and right behind the stand you have a really nice watering hole.

We see some does throughout the day into the evening, and then it’s the last hour of daylight and we see a buck way off. There are some does right up on the hill that this food plot leads up to, and he bumps one of those does down. She comes down into the food plot pretty close to us, like 30-ish yards. And then he’s up there on this hill, sun going down, perfect golden-hour lighting, just looking unbelievably majestic. Oh, and by the way, I have a camera guy over my shoulder filming all this.

So then he follows that doe right down into the plot. I had ranged little empty spots in the food plot, or little shadows, earlier in the day, but now it’s last light. There are no shadows.

Scott: But also my brain was not working. I don’t know exactly what my thought process was, but I was at full draw, and I dropped my 35 pin behind the shoulder and shot. As soon as the arrow hit, it was like, ugh, because it did not penetrate even a little bit. You could just see it hanging out. And he bounds off and stands at 60 yards.

Scott: Yeah, a high shoulder hit. And he’s standing there right at 60, looking around, not sure what just happened. He stood there for a while, and then he just walks off into the woods. And I was just like, “What just happened?” I think everyone knows that thick feeling when you know you just screwed up big time — especially because it was a great deer, a really nice, tall 8-point.

So what had happened is I shot him for 35, and he was 30. And looking back at the slow-motion footage, he dropped a few inches. Also, his leg that was closest to me was back, and that arrow hit the upper portion of the scapula — there’s that hard ridge right there. The arrow hit that bone square. So it didn’t even hit the soft part of the scapula, where you might have a chance. It hit right on that bone. I would imagine that deer survived. We looked all the next day, and we didn’t find anything but a few drops of blood.

Alex: Yeah, that’s a nonlethal hit with archery equipment pretty much every time. You’re just kind of screwed. That’s not where you want to shoot a deer, you know?

Scott: No. If you’re trying to kill one, that’s not the spot to hit them.

Scott: And to make matters worse, I’ve been a fan of archery my whole life, and Levi Morgan is the guy in 3D archery — definitely the greatest of the current generation, and in the conversation for greatest 3D archer of all time. And he’s across the field watching this with some other guys, and their binoculars all go down. Oh, no. So someone you look up to is watching you screw up. Even worse.

Alex: Yeah. And he has you on his property to hunt these big deer. And you’re like, “I’m an Outdoor Life archery guy. I can do this. I’ve bowhunted my entire life. This is my thing.”

Scott: Yeah. And there were a lot of things I did wrong there, obviously. I think the moment was so big — this really cool sequence of events — and I just didn’t take the second to range. My rangefinder was right there. I could’ve just clicked and confirmed, but in the moment I was like, “Yep, that’s 35, maybe.” That little short circuit is ultimately what it was, because the shot-execution part was fine.

Alex: It’s not like you hit far back. You basically hit where you were aiming, right? You were just aiming with the wrong pin, or you were not holding low enough.

Scott: Yeah. It’s the dumbest of all mistakes to make.

Alex: Going back to the unpressured deer, one thing that I have noticed — especially with more mature bucks in the rut — is you can get away with so much more than we often think. Especially if you’re used to hunting deer earlier in the year, or shooting does, where any little movement or any little mistake and their attention is on you. There have been times where I’ve tried to stop a buck with the classic “meh” to get them to stop walking so I can shoot, and they’re 20 yards away and they don’t stop. I’ve had to yell to get their attention, because they’re just in that rut mode.

And I guess my point is I’ve made mistakes of being in the tree and thinking, “OK, I can’t range. I need to just shoot, because if I try to range and then draw, he’s going to see me draw, and I just have to make this shot.” Oftentimes you can range. Even if the buck’s in the open, you can draw, and maybe they see you and stop and then you can shoot them, or maybe they don’t even see you.

Scott: Yeah. And it was also an open field, so it’s not like you could range some trees and have real landmarks — which I guess I’m not very used to. I don’t hunt a lot of open fields. But talking to Levi this year about what he does in the tree when a buck is coming in, he has his rangefinder in his hand and is ranging the deer as it’s coming in, thinking about all the possible places where that buck could end up in front of him. He’s one of the best people in the world at judging distance, and he’s still ranging the deer as it comes in until he gets a shot.

Alex: Yeah. A world-champion 3D archer is doing this.

Scott: Yes. And he said he wants to know the exact distance that deer is at before he pulls back his bow.

Alex: On my tree harness, I have a little clip that I clip my rangefinder to, so I can range and then just drop it, and it stays on my harness. I don’t have to shove it back in my pocket or take it out. Honestly, I started doing that after a similar situation to yours. I shot a buck that was closer than I thought, and because of that, I didn’t hit him well and didn’t get him. And I was like, “OK, now I need to range every shot, unless it’s obviously 20 yards or closer.”

Scott: Yeah. And I’ve also started aiming a little lower. I was aiming mid-body behind the shoulder, but now I’m aiming at the top of the heart, especially on those closer shots.

Alex: OK. So let’s move to this year. What was your hunt like this year? How’d that play out?

Scott: So this year, we hit a cold front just as we were arriving. It was pretty incredible, actually, to have that timing — perfect weather, ideal conditions. The deer were chasing. You could see it all on the trail cameras from 10 a.m. until 3 p.m. Bucks everywhere.

Scott: The day that we arrived, we were planning on trying to get out in the stand. We all got there around noon, but we were like, “We can’t, because there are deer everywhere and we’ll just end up bumping them. It’s better to sneak in in the morning and then hunt.” And so that’s what we did.

One really cool thing that I’ve learned from Levi and Andy is how to hunt deer without them knowing that they’re being hunted. They are very particular about their entry and exit routes into the stands — getting in clean, getting out clean, in terms of wind direction, ground scent and just not bumping deer on your way to a stand location. So they have some really cool, sneaky spots where you can very easily get in and get out.

The one I was hunting, there are these train tracks that run through a portion of the property, and they have three stands right off the train tracks. You drive a side-by-side down the train tracks, go maybe 50 yards into the woods, and you’re up a tree. So it’s real easy, with no chance of really bumping anything, and you just sit there all day. For the most part, they’re on pinch points between food and bedding, or on natural travel corridors. I mean, there isn’t a bad spot on this property, but these ones in particular are very, very cool.

Alex: I have a quick question on that. You have all this camera activity and you’re getting pictures of all these bucks, and obviously some places are going to be a little harder to access than others. And then you have these train-track stands that are super sneaky to get in and out of. I feel like I know the answer to this, but if there’s one camera that has a giant buck on it, but there’s a probability of spooking deer on that access, versus these other cameras where you know you can get in clean and out clean — which one are they going to send you to?

Scott: The ones you can get in and out clean.

Alex: Even though you only have a few days to hunt, they’re like, “No matter what, we’re not going to spook deer.”

Scott: Pretty much. For example, that stand I hunted last year — this year, Levi shot a really nice buck out of that same stand. And right after that, there were more big bucks on that same food plot every single day. But nobody hunted it, because you can’t get in there in the morning without bumping them. It’s a food plot, and the only access is to walk down the edge of the woods. The other problem is the wind direction ended up switching. So you’d have to try to get in there in the middle of the day, but the deer were so active in the middle of the day that that whole really awesome spot with good deer on it didn’t end up being huntable.

Another part of this approach is they’re really hunting the outer perimeter of the property and not going right into the middle. Last year we had trail cameras down in these creek bottoms, and it was like a deer highway, especially in the middle of the day — big bucks just cruising up and down. But we didn’t hunt them, because there’s too great a chance of getting busted in there. When the thermals switch, the wind has to be so perfect that it’s not worth the risk of going right into the middle of the property and trying to kill a deer, because you’re going to blow the whole property out on that one attempt. Maybe if it was just your property you could do whatever you want, but there are other people trying to kill bucks at the same time.

Alex: So the reason the deer are the way they are is, one, because it’s only hunted two weeks out of the year. But two, the way that it’s hunted, the deer don’t even feel the pressure that they have on them, because they’re just not bumping into humans or human scent.

Scott: Right. And in the places where they are — I mean, it’s an active farm. They’re used to seeing people on the farm roads and stuff.

Scott: And just to hit that point a little bit more: When you do bump a deer going in, if you’re accessing through an area where they’re used to seeing people, those deer will be right back.

Alex: Yeah. It’s not like you’re bumping them out of their bedding area or their main feeding area. Got it. All right, go on with your hunt for this year.

Scott: So back to the redemption day. I’m in this stand. Another thing about hunting with Levi and Andy is they like to hang their stands very high. One of the guys got into one and ranged it, and it was 12 or 13 yards to the bottom of the tree. So like 36 feet in the air. They’re not all that high, but they’re all at least 20 feet up.

Alex: Why do they do that? For scent, or so you don’t get seen, or they just like it?

Scott: A little bit of both. I talked to Levi about this last year. It’s just how he grew up hunting. His dad always hung the stands really high, because he’s from North Carolina, where deer actually do look up into trees as they walk. So this is what he’s used to and what he’s always done. And Levi’s also really tall. He’s 6-foot-4. So if you’re shorter than 6-foot-4, you might have to make some jumps as you climb up the sticks, because of the gap between the sticks. Luckily I didn’t have that problem.

Alex: OK. So somehow you made it way high up there.

Scott: I’m high up in the tree. I’ve got a camera guy with me, and the stand looks higher than it is because it’s up on a hill, and you’re looking down at a couple trails that are at the bottom of this hill. So it’s a pretty steep downward angle.

The morning was pretty quiet for the most part. That first hour of daylight, I saw some deer, nothing crazy. Saw a coyote. Heard the most amazing turkey vocalizations of all time — a huge group of hens behind us, everything in the book. It was nuts, and loud. So that was cool for me. And then we had an 8-point come in at about 15 yards — a really nice, maybe 3-year-old typical 8-point. But the camera guy couldn’t get on him. And I mean, it’s the first morning.

Scott: Yeah. I’m not used to passing a deer like that, but I did. It felt weird. And the morning just goes on. We hear some deer fighting behind us. I see some bucks cruising the ridge ahead of us, about 100 yards out. And then it goes quiet, and I start eating every snack and sandwich I packed. Getting a little sleepy — it’s 12 o’clock, the sun’s on me. I’d packed a heavier jacket, so I throw it on, and I’m kind of nodding off, not really paying attention.

And then all of a sudden, the woods erupt in front of us, and two does come barreling down into this bottom. I’m trying to get my stuff together and stand up out of this — I was in a Millennium stand, so I was very comfortable — trying to sit up and grab my bow off the hanger. And then I’m looking for whatever buck is going to be coming in after them.

Alex: Can I ask you a quick question? When you have deer come in and you’re pretty sure it’s a buck, do you stand up or do you stay sitting down?

Scott: In this stand, because of the shot angle, you definitely had to be standing to bend over for that shot. But the year before, there was a limb that came up right where my top cam was, so I had to sit and shoot, which I’m not used to.

So I get stood up. There are some deer coming off to the left now. I see another doe come running in, and I’m looking for the buck that’s chasing these. And then I see this tall 8-point that has tines that almost come in and touch. He’s the one that I had seen on the trail cameras leading up to this trip. I’d actually talked to Levi about him the day before, as we were discussing all the cool deer: “Man, I really, really like that unique 8-point look.” And it’s him — on the complete opposite side of the farm from where I had seen him the day before.

Scott: Yep. So he’s coming in. I had ranged some trees ahead of time, and there are pretty much two trails he could have walked in on: one that goes from 30 to 20 yards in front of the stand, and one that goes right under the stand. He’s standing right by the one that goes from 30 to 20, and I know I’m going to shoot him with either my top pin or my second pin. So I come to full draw, thinking he’s going to step out and turn broadside any second. And he’s just standing there, and I’m at full draw thinking, “What is this dude going to do?” And he turns and walks to the closer trail, which none of the does had walked in on.

Now he’s going to be coming in about 10 yards from me. I’m at full draw for what felt like forever, but it was totally fine, with a giant buck in front of me. He’s walking, and I give him the bleat, and he does not stop. I do a louder one, and then he stops, and I drop my top pin just above the midline on his body, since it’s such a steep angle. And the shot goes off. I was shooting a resistance release, and it went off very easily. And I see about half an arrow’s worth of penetration, and I’m like, “Not again.”

Alex: Oh, no. Did it feel like you hit where you aimed?

Scott: I honestly don’t remember. I’m just glad it was 10 yards. Maybe we got lucky there. The deer runs off, and then we hear him crash. I’m looking at the camera guy, and I’m not ready to celebrate, because I’m not feeling 100 percent confident in the shot. Typically I’m used to passing through deer, with either compounds or recurves, especially at that distance. But we heard him crash, so I felt pretty good about it.

It takes me a while to settle down, and we climb down. I don’t find any blood where I shot him, but we start walking in the direction we heard him crash, and there he was, lying there 40 yards away — dead as a doornail.

Scott: Basically what happened is the arrow came in high, right behind the shoulder, and then exited at the armpit on the offside and hit the elbow bone on that offside shoulder.

Scott: Yeah. The broadhead was just poking through the skin on the offside. So luckily he crashed close, because that would’ve been a tough one to track.

Alex: So basically two years of hunting this place, and you walk up on this deer. You made your shot. How does that feel?

Scott: It took me a while for it to fully sink in, because hunting in the rut, things happen so quickly. I was about to take a nap, and two minutes later this deer is there. It was a huge weight off my shoulders. I got to have a drama-free experience of finding the deer. Everything went great on that end. And then Levi and Andy came in the side-by-side, we picked him up, and it was just like, “Man, what a relief.” But at the same time, I was like, “I really want to spend more time in this stand.”

The day after, I couldn’t get into the stand to try to fill my doe tag, but I ended up hanging stands with Levi and Andy on one of their new leases, and that was awesome. We found such a cool spot, and I got to watch how they approach picking a tree and that on-the-run scouting. I mean, that was worth the price of not going hunting that day. I would much rather do that.

Alex: What was your biggest takeaway from watching those guys? They know an area’s good, but what’s the next step for narrowing it down to, “OK, this tree is where we’re going to hang it”?

Scott: Andy calls it structure, because he’s a pro bass fisherman, so it’s terminology he’s familiar with. Basically what they’re looking for is little things that will funnel deer movement closer to your stand location, but also give you a backstop for your wind direction — like, deer won’t be coming from here, so we can hunt it on this wind. The way he puts it is you’re always giving up something. There’s not one perfect wind direction. You always have that risk, but you’re trying to minimize it and at the same time funnel deer past your stand location.

In this case, there’s an ag field maybe 60 yards in front of the stand. Then in the woods behind you, there’s a really thick brier patch that deer won’t walk through. But there’s an opening in the brier patch, and an old two-track that comes in also. You could just see the deer trails funneling right through this spot that they found. Then you find the right tree to hang it in. It was cool. We saw a couple of really good deer while we were hanging that stand, so it’ll be a good one for next year. But those guys are always hanging more stands. I think they must have hung a few while we were there — more wind-direction options.

Alex: You had this whitetail wonderland experience, but what do you think your main takeaways are coming back to the real world and hunting regular places like the rest of us? What’s applicable?

Scott: I mean, the entry and exit thing is something that I’ve applied to how I hunt my lease. I wish my lease neighbor did the same. But just being mindful of the pressure you’re putting on it going in, going out, and while you’re in the stand — where your scent cone is blowing.

I still need to get better at staying present and task-focused when a big buck comes barreling in on you. Hunting during the rut can definitely leave you a little flat-footed sometimes. I think that’s just more experience than anything else, because I’m more used to hunting deer over food sources, where you have a little more time to get warmed up to the idea of killing this deer.

Alex: Right. So many times in the rut, you hear a buck coming, then you see him for a few seconds, and then you have to shoot. You have to decide that he’s a buck you want to shoot, and you have to decide how you’re going to shoot him and where, all in a matter of a few seconds. And like you said, you could’ve been about to take a nap or eat a sandwich 30 seconds before that, you know?

Read Next: How I Beat Bowhunting Buck Fever and Snapped My Big Buck Losing Streak

Scott: Yeah, for sure. And I got pictures last night of a really great deer on my lease. I mean, it was 9:30 at night, but I still have another month to find that deer and get him killed.

Alex: All right, Scott. Well, thank you for the insight and for sharing this little window into the perfect corner of whitetail hunting country. We can all live vicariously through you.

Scott: Yes. If I never get invited back, I won’t be too sad.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8248. 3 Totally Normal Deer Hunting Tactics We Used to Think Were Utter Nonsense

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 25, 2026 1:22 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

When they were first introduced to the national hunting community, these novel methods for bringing in bucks were considered unconventional at best, and harebrained schemes by most. Now deer hunters everywhere use these tried-and-true tactics. We take a look back to when these trusty standbys were still considered downright bizarre.

The brush-country hunters of Texas and New Mexico were crashing antlers together for decades before the trend caught fire in the rest of whitetail country. Although Native hunters almost certainly developed the technique, legend has it that an old market hunter accidentally discovered the phenomenon.

“He was coming to town one day, his wagon loaded with deer carcasses, when a buck came barging out of the mesquite,” reads one May 1951 story from OL. “The hunter, so the story goes, added him to the load. A short time later, another buck pranced up — and was soon in the wagon. The puzzled hunter stopped to figure things out and discovered that two carcasses were lying so their antlers clashed as the wagon jounced along the rough country road.”

Related: How to Rattle in a Buck, Based on Whitetail Deer Research

Our first story devoted to rattling appeared in October 1937. A Texas game warden, drawing on 30 years of experience with the tactic, taught author Fredric P. Schwab exactly how to sound like “two bucks in a life-and-death struggle.”

By the 1950s, most hunters in the rest of the country had heard of rattling, but few had tried it. Almost everyone who had tried tickling tines reported the method didn’t work on hill-country deer, although a rare hunter outside the Lone-Star State would claim success. Here’s what modern research says about the efficacy of rattling in deer.

The concept of calling for deer was less established even than rattling in the middle of the 20th century. In August 1949, an experienced deer hunter traveled to Alaska for a Sitka blacktail hunt. “He was sure it was just a gag,” reads the story. “Who ever head of calling a buck?”

“Now I’ve used crow calls, duck calls, and turkey calls, and I’d read that down in Texas they lure bucks by rattling a couple of antlers together. But a real deer call I’d never heard of. Probably my voice expressed my skepticism. ‘O.K. I’ll bite. What’s a deer call?’”

Read Now: When and How to Use a Grunt Tube to Call in Deer

The Alaskan hunters employed the call often — which looks a bit like a harmonica and sounds like “a lost lamb bleating for its mother,” — but they admit they don’t know what sound it was supposed to replicate. “I’ve attracted does as well as bucks, so I don’t think it’s a mating call,” said one local. “An old Indian told me it’s the cry of a fawn in mortal terror,” said another.

In the end, the author and a fellow hunter call in two bucks and drop both of them. This story, “A Deer Call Brings ‘Em In!” garnered so much reader mail that an advice column on using commercial calls appeared in the August 1949 issue. The expert claimed to have used his call with excellent results on 100 wild deer, and that his call was a modern counterpart of those made by Native Americans in Alaska. So while calls were being produced commercially by the late 40s, they remained news to most hunters.

Although a variety of products designed to lure bucks and cover up human odor had been marketed for years, it appears most hunters initially considered the scents for sale at the local sporting goods shop akin to something hawked by a snake oil salesman.

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work for Deer Hunting

“It was probably because I was growing desperate that I decided to buy the deer scent,” writes John Weiss, author of the November 1978 feature “Scents and Nonscents.” “I figured there was nothing to lose.”

Weiss reported that more than 50 companies made scents at the time, and were raking in an estimated $37 million a year. That included everything from hunter’s soaps and food attractants to tarsal scents and urine.

He then delved into the types of scents and their effectiveness, and dug into the “scientific” realm of deer hunting. Interestingly, most biologists interviewed for the story disregarded “a deer’s scenting ability as not all that important.” One researcher noted that a deer’s “visual capabilities are far more refined than hearing or smelling abilities.”

Yet most wildlife biologists today agree that a deer’s nose is it’s most formidable asset. Nonscents, indeed. It makes you wonder: If these are the facts we believed back then, just think about what we’ve got wrong now. And, even more fun to imagine, is what idiotic tactic might be all the rage in another couple decades.

This story, “‘Wacky’ Deer Tactics,” first appeared in the Oct. 2015 issue of Outdoor Life.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.
